claims.text: Replacing an EAM thermodynamic-integration reference with an MLIP trained on diverse ab initio liquid configurations will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
Replacing the EAM reference with the liquid-trained MLIP will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch for high-temperature HEAs.
The intended systems include refractory multicomponent alloys containing elements such as W, Ta, Hf, Nb, and Ti.
The relevant melting-temperature range for these refractory HEAs is approximately 3000–4000 K.
The intervention is intended to apply to both solid and fully disordered liquid states.
Moment-tensor and deep-neural-network potentials are candidate MLIP reference forms.
The MLIP should be trained on a comprehensive set of ab initio molecular-dynamics trajectories of the liquid.
The intervention is applicable to equiatomic or near-equiatomic refractory HEAs near 3000–4000 K.
Configurational disorder is large in the stated equiatomic or near-equiatomic systems.
Many-body descriptors and diverse liquid training configurations allow the MLIP to capture the full spectrum of local atomic arrangements and vibrational modes.
Capturing those arrangements and modes bridges the configurational landscape between the ab initio liquid and the reference state.
Conventional EAM potentials are limited in representing the many atomic configurations present in a high-temperature disordered liquid.
An MLIP trained on ab initio liquid data accounts for many-body effects and liquid fluctuations better than an EAM reference.
Better representation of many-body effects and liquid fluctuations enhances reference–target phase-space overlap and narrows the integration-path mismatch.
The MLIP reference will reduce integration-path mismatch by roughly 50% relative to conventional EAM references.
Reduced path mismatch will produce more accurate thermodynamic-integration free-energy differences between liquid and solid phases.
TOR-TILD relies on conventional EAM references that inadequately sample ab initio-liquid configurations and consequently exhibit significant integration-path mismatch.
The effectiveness of the MLIP reference may be reduced by extreme local ordering, phase separation, or incomplete training data.
The approximately 50% mismatch-reduction estimate is based on analogies with elemental and binary systems.
Failure to obtain at least a 30% statistically significant reduction in path mismatch and associated error, or failure to improve phase-space-overlap metrics, would falsify the hypothesis.
